source.title: Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias? Looking for Optimal Inductive Biases in the Wild
source.authors: Damien Teney; Liang-Ze Jiang; Florin Gogianu; Ehsan Abbasnejad

record.tranche_reason: The study changes activation functions to alter architectural inductive biases and measures effects on test accuracy, but it does not test any listed version's specific intervention or measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy outcomes for learned activations on image and tabular tasks. Shortcut-learning and grokking results are excluded because they concern OOD or algorithmic generalization, which the claim separates.
record.test_reason: The study tests activation-induced simplicity biases, not V1–V8. Its width experiments do not establish interpolation or continued improvement beyond zero training error; its complexity landscapes measure output total variation, not magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: ReLU simplicity bias is near-optimal for the tested image-classification tasks but suboptimal in some regression, tabular, shortcut-learning, and algorithmic settings. Learned activations can improve performance by changing inductive biases. The authors do not claim simplicity bias is generally ineffective.
record.recipe_differences: The study meta-learns dataset-specific activation functions and compares their test performance with ReLU models; it does not reproduce the methods in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and task type change the outcome: gains are small on image classification, while learned activations improve results on tabular tasks. The paper also reports different best complexity levels across tabular datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned activations provide little improvement over ReLUs on image classification, with slight gains on SVHN and CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset-specific learned activations offer limited accuracy benefits over ReLUs on these image-classification tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: On tabular classification tasks, learned activations close the performance gap to boosted trees; input activations perform best and sometimes surpass trees.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changing activation-induced inductive biases can improve tabular MLP accuracy relative to ReLU and tree baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned activations improve image-regression performance, with higher output-function complexity associated with better accuracy in these experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some regression tasks benefit from activation functions that permit more complex input-output mappings.

fits_no_version.finding: The study examines total variation of model outputs and complexity near trained parameters, rather than perturbation-induced increases in training error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation choices alter the complexity of functions represented near trained solutions.

record.problems: The paper prioritizes breadth and uses simple MLPs; it notes that additional hyperparameter tuning could improve model performance. Main image and tabular comparisons are reported qualitatively in the supplied text, without exact per-dataset values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Shortcut-learning collage results in Sections 3.4 and E.5 are OOD; algorithmic grokking results in Sections 3.5 and E.6 concern algorithmic tasks. Both are outside the claim's stated scope.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error beyond the width required for zero training error. Width sweeps are reported, but interpolation thresholds and training to convergence are not established.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Large versus small batches under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is warranted for V1–V8. The excluded shortcut and grokking findings also do not measure these versions. Their exclusion follows the specific version definitions, rather than a blanket exclusion of OOD or algorithmic generalization.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label performance under the same recipe.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation for the stated one-hidden-layer ReLU setup.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning or recovery conditions.
Large versus small batch effects on the generalization gap under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing influential memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: MLPs with learned activation functions
rows.operation_detail: Replace ReLU activation with a learned activation function, initialized as ReLU or zeros.

conditions.value: MNIST, FASHION-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR; classification tasks

rows.baseline: ReLU models perform similarly; exact values not stated in text.
rows.value: Differences are small; learned activations only improve slightly on SVHN and CIFAR.
rows.note: The text gives an aggregate qualitative comparison across image classification datasets, without separate values per dataset.
rows.check: This is the study's activation-learning method compared with ReLU baselines, not a test of a listed version. The qualitative accuracy comparison is correct. However, Appendix E.2 says the main results select the best depth from 1–4 hidden layers for each activation, so describing all reported results as a fixed 3-layer architecture is incomplete. Replacing activations before training is also not a post-training weight edit.

rows.subject: MLPs with learned activation functions (AFs) and input activation functions (IAFs)
rows.size_stated: MLPs with 1–4 hidden layers; width 256 stated in experimental details
rows.operation_detail: Use learned activation functions or input activation functions instead of standard ReLU activations.
rows.baseline: Vanilla MLPs generally perform worse than trees.
rows.value: Learned activations eliminate the gap to trees; IAFs perform best, sometimes surpassing trees.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result across 16 datasets; the paper also says accuracy peaks at different complexity levels on different datasets.
rows.check: This aggregates the study's method-performance comparisons across datasets and activation configurations; it should not be a claim-evidence row for V1–V8. The qualitative result is supported, but input activations transform individual input dimensions before the MLP rather than simply replacing its hidden ReLUs. Neither the tree comparison nor the activation comparison measures a listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
